title: Async communication with queues
idea: A queue sits between services. The sender adds a message and moves on; a consumer processes it later, at its own pace.
points: Messages wait in the queue when consumers are down or slow.
Add more consumers to drain a backlog; the sender does not change.
Normally a message is deleted only after the consumer acknowledges it (an ack).
No ack means redelivery, so delivery is at-least-once and duplicates can happen.

hero.title: A job, a missing ack, a second delivery

messages.label: enqueue job 7
messages.note: The API puts a job on the queue and replies to the user at once. It does not wait for the work.

messages.label: deliver job 7
messages.note: The queue hands job 7 to worker 1. It keeps its own copy until the worker sends an ack.

messages.label: slow, no ack yet
messages.note: Worker 1 is slow, or its connection dropped. The ack does not arrive in time.

messages.label: redeliver job 7
messages.note: The queue cannot tell slow from dead, so it delivers job 7 again, to worker 2. This is at-least-once delivery.

messages.label: ack job 7
messages.note: Worker 2 finishes and sends the ack. The queue now deletes job 7.

messages.label: finishes job 7 too
messages.note: Worker 1 finishes too, so the work ran twice. A handler is idempotent if running it twice equals running it once.

code.title: An idempotent handler
code.caption: The handler remembers job ids, so a repeat is skipped. Delete the `done.has` line and run again.

pitfalls: Do not assume a message arrives once; record handled ids in shared storage.
Acknowledge only after the work succeeds; an early ack loses the job on a crash.
Watch queue depth: a growing backlog means consumers cannot keep up.

quiz.q: This handler has no duplicate check. The ack for j2 is lost. What prints?
options: email for j1, email for j2
email for j1, email for j2, skip j2
email for j1, skip j1, email for j2
email for j1, email for j2, email for j2
quiz.why: The lost ack makes the queue deliver j2 again. With no duplicate check, the handler runs twice and sends a second email.

takeaway: A queue decouples services, but delivery is at-least-once: make handlers idempotent.

starters: What is the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once delivery?
Where do messages go when a consumer keeps failing?
Which tools implement queues, such as RabbitMQ or SQS?
